1:
Gill fixes the moment. This comes after the murmuring over the spies' report, after the sentence that the generation should be consumed in the wilderness, and after the defeat at Hormah — spoken lest their posterity should be discouraged and despair of ever enjoying the good land. Keil measures the silence that follows it. After the attempt to force an entry into Canaan against the will of God and the advice of Moses, the Israelites remained many days in Kadesh, then turned into the wilderness toward the Red Sea as they had been commanded, and did not come again to the desert of Zin until the first month of the fortieth year. All we know of that interval is a list of encampment names, and since the situation of most of them is unknown, or at any rate undetermined, no connected account of Israel's movements through those thirty-seven years can be given. Henry hears in the law's opening words an answer to the sentence. When you come into the land of your habitation which I give unto you is a plain intimation not only that God was reconciled to them notwithstanding what he had just decreed, but that he would secure the promised land to their seed notwithstanding their proneness to rebel; the statute takes it for granted that some of them should in due time come into Canaan.

Calvin explains what the meal and drink offerings are doing attached to every sacrifice. In these oblations God consulted the rude condition of the people and took, as it were, the character of a man, as if he feasted familiarly with them — which is why he elsewhere calls the sacrifices his meat, not because he who is the life in himself and inspires the life of all requires the supports of life, but because unless he descends to men he cannot lift up their minds to things above. Henry says the same thing domestically. Since the sacrifices of acknowledgment were meant as the food of God's table, there had to be a constant provision of bread and oil and wine whatever the flesh-meat was; it was fit that God should keep a good house, that his table should be furnished with bread as well as flesh, and that his cup should run over — in my Father's house there is bread enough.

The measures are the point of the chapter, and Calvin gives two reasons for them. The first is editorial: Moses partly adverts here to precepts handled more fully in Leviticus and partly gathers into one place what he had said in various places and more obscurely, since as yet no certain regulation had been given about the accessories of oil and wine, and what had been appropriated to particular cases is now commanded generally. The second is the real one. There was danger on the other side lest the people should introduce many inane and superfluous pomps — as the Gentiles were foolishly and immoderately luxurious in their sacred feasts, as if their delicacies gave pleasure to God — and so the measure of each particular thing is prescribed, that they may not dare to invent anything arbitrarily. The ceremonies might be of trifling importance in themselves, but the lawful had to be carefully distinguished from the unauthorized, to forestall the licentiousness of men, who would otherwise not have failed to mingle their own leaven. Henry draws the plain moral from the tables of quantities: our religious services should be governed, as by other rules, so by the rule of proportion.
2:
Gill identifies the audience narrowly. Those of twenty years old and upward had been sworn to die in the wilderness; the people Moses is told to address are the younger sort, who should actually possess the land. Wesley hears the promise inside the preamble — I give you means I will certainly give you, notwithstanding this great provocation, and for their better assurance God repeats and amplifies the laws of sacrifice by which he would be reconciled to them and theirs upon their repentance. Clarke adds a practical reason for the future tense: some learned men are of opinion that several offerings prescribed by the law were never intended to be made in the wilderness at all, which did not afford the conveniences the worship required, but only in the promised land.

The chapter's substance is a table of quantities, and Wesley states the principle it embodies in a sentence — two tenth deals for the ram because it belonged to a better sacrifice than the lamb, and three for the bullock after it, so that the accessory sacrifice grows proportionably with the principal. He converts the measures as well: a tenth deal is the tenth part of an ephah, about five pints, and a hin about five quarts. Ellicott places the rule among its neighbours, the meal and drink offerings ordered here for a lamb being the same as those appointed to accompany the morning and evening lamb, and offerings of this kind having already been prescribed in connection with the three great feasts. Gill notes that the wine had to be wine of the grapes, on the Targum's authority, no other sort being permissible for the purpose. Keil draws the arithmetic out — the number of appointed quantities was to correspond to the number of sacrificial animals — and pauses over a grammatical oddity, a third-person verb standing between two second-person forms, which he calls certainly striking and unusual, but not so offensive as to make it necessary to alter the text.

Then the clause that sets two commentators against each other: one law for you and for the stranger. Gill and Calvin agree on who is meant, not the stranger of the gate but the proselyte of righteousness, and Calvin states the limit plainly, that those who remained in uncircumcision were excluded by their uncleanness from the legal service. But Calvin reads the single form as a guard for uniformity, and gives two reasons for it: that proselytes lately incorporated might devote themselves the more cheerfully to piety when they saw themselves placed in the same position as the children of Abraham, and that if any distinction were made, corrupt mixtures would immediately creep in — so that lest the purity of God's worship should be gradually corrupted by absurd imitation, the gate was shut against the variety which usually draws men aside in different directions. Clarke draws the opposite conclusion from the same verse. One form of worship was a necessity in that land, surrounded as it was by idolatrous nations, and it was right that those who conformed should have equal rights and privileges, as indeed they did; but under the Christian dispensation no particular form is prescribed and the types are fulfilled, so unlimited toleration should be allowed, and while the sacred writings are made the basis of the worship offered to God, every man should be permitted to worship according to his own conscience. Wesley takes a third line, that the equality is religious and not civil: the stranger's sacrifices were offered in the same manner and accepted on the same terms, a presage of the future calling of the Gentiles, but he adds the caution that strangers were not on this pretence to partake of Israel's civil privileges.
17:
The law binds Israelites only. Gill reports the rabbinic ruling that follows from it — the dough of a Gentile is free from the cake, even though an Israelite kneads it. On the timing both he and Wesley are exact: the offering falls not after the eating but before it, when they are about to eat, the corn ground into flour and the flour mixed and kneaded into dough ready for the oven. By bread, Gill adds, is meant bread corn, and specifically the old corn of the land which they first ate on entering it; the Targum excludes rice and millet and pulse, and the Jewish authorities name five grains only from which the cake was required — wheat, barley, rye, a second kind of barley, and oats. The obligation covers dough made for men's bread and no other, not what is baked for dogs or any beast.

The quantity is the interesting silence. Gill observes that the text does not express it at all, leaving it to the people's generosity, with no stinted measure fixed by the law; it is tradition rather than statute that supplies the figure, and the traditions of the elders make the cake the twenty-fourth part of the first dough kneaded — not the forty-fourth, Gill notes, as Buxtorf through mistake says. The Targum agrees at one part in twenty-four, and so does the Mishnah, though it lowers the share to a forty-eighth for dough made to be sold publicly. Gill records one more attempt at the number, which rests on the spelling: because the word begins and ends with the letter that stands numerically for forty, some have taken it as an instruction to the bountiful man to give a fortieth. Ellicott confines himself to the word itself, which may be rendered mixed meal, is used only in the plural, and outside these two verses occurs only twice in the whole Old Testament.

Why the offering is made of dough rather than grain is Calvin's question, and his answer is the best line in the passage. First-fruits were already offered of their fruits and their ears of corn, but the representation was more lively in the bread itself; God would therefore have them present tokens of their gratitude not only from the barn but from the mill and the oven, so that while they were eating their bread also they might have him before their eyes. Gill reads the gesture the same way, as an acknowledgment that God is the sovereign Lord and possessor of heaven and earth and the owner and proprietor of the land of Canaan, and as thankfulness for the plenty of bread corn he had given them — which is why the cake was to be heaved, lifted up toward him in heaven.
22:
Gill begins by widening the word. Every sin is an error, a missing of the mark, a wandering from the way of God's commandments; and though Jarchi and the Jewish writers generally take this passage of idolatry, it rather respects any deviation from the law, moral or ceremonial, and especially the latter. Calvin sharpens it in the other direction, toward something more culpable than accident: the word extends to incogitancy, which partakes of contempt of God and arises from too great security, when men inconsiderately fall into the sins their lusts invite them to — which is why deliberate impiety is set against it afterwards, when men designedly rush into violations of the law. Ellicott fixes the technical sense, that shegagah denotes transgressions committed unwittingly, standing in contrast to the sin done presumptuously later in the chapter.

Why the law is given again at all, Leviticus having already provided for sins of ignorance, is the question the commentators divide over. Wesley answers that the earlier statute speaks of a positive miscarriage, of doing about the holy things of God what ought not to have been done, whereas this speaks only of an omission of something that ought to have been done about holy ceremonies. Ellicott reaches the same distinction from the other side — provision had been made for sins of commission unwittingly committed by the whole congregation, but none appears to have been made for the guilt contracted by sins of omission — and adds two observations in support: the offerings differ, a young bullock being the sin offering there while here the bullock is a burnt offering and a kid the sin offering; and the commandments of this chapter have express reference to the land of Canaan, whereas many delivered earlier were already binding. Clarke divides the material differently again, taking the case here to refer to the whole congregation and the cases just before to the sin of an individual. Calvin sees no new law at all, only a relaxation: two bullocks were commanded before, one for a burnt offering and one for a sin offering, and permission is given here to substitute a goat if the second were not easily obtained, so that Leviticus delivers the regular and perfect rite while this passage adds the permissive alteration.

What the provision is for, Calvin states best. Since nothing is easier than for men to err, the remedy was most necessary, lest those who had sinned should fall into despair; so that when the people or private persons saw their guilt, and might have despaired of pardon and thrown away the pursuit of holiness, God anticipates them and shews by what means he is to be propitiated, that the sins which had occurred should not interrupt his service. Henry keeps both halves of the balance. Sins committed ignorantly still need atoning for, since ignorance will in a degree excuse but will not justify those who might have known their Lord's will and did it not, which is why David prayed to be cleansed from his secret faults, the errors he did not himself understand. And they are forgiven, through the great sacrifice, who when he offered himself once for all upon the cross seemed to explain the intention of that offering in the prayer, Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do; Paul alludes to this same law when he says he obtained mercy because he did it ignorantly and in unbelief. Henry notes too what looked favourably on the Gentiles, that this atonement for ignorance is expressly extended to those who were strangers to the commonwealth of Israel; and Keil confirms the reach of it, that the rule laid down for Israelites is here raised into general validity for foreigners as well.
30:
What the phrase means is settled quickly. Ellicott gives it literally — with a high hand — and corrects the verb that follows, which is not reproacheth but blasphemeth. Gill fills in the manner from the Targum's through pride: haughty, insolent, bold and daring, obstinate and self-willed, done with purpose and design, openly and publicly, neither fearing God nor regarding man. Henry defines it by intent rather than by degree. Presumptuous sinners are those who avowedly confront God's authority and set up their own lust in competition with it, who sin for sinning's sake in contradiction to the precept and in defiance of the penalty, who fight against God and dare him to do his worst; it is not only to sin against knowledge but to sin designedly against God's will and glory. Wesley reduces it to the insult it contains: the man sets God at defiance and exposes him to contempt, as if he were unable to punish transgressors.

Calvin agrees about the posture and then narrows the offence sharply. To deal with a high hand is nothing more than to attempt or undertake proudly what is not lawful, since our hands ought to be guided and as it were restrained by God's word, lest they lift themselves up. But although men's hands are used in many acts of audacity, what is meant here in particular is the profanation of God's true and legitimate worship, when anything is invented inconsistent with its purity: the punishment is not decreed against thefts or murders or other such crimes, but against the perverse imaginations which tend to the corruption of religion. All self-invented services betray an impious contempt of God, as if men designedly despised him and spurned at his commands; whence Calvin infers that nothing is more opposed to perfect and sincere religion than the temerity which induces men to follow whatever course they please. Gill marks what the reason clause does not mean: the presumptuous man has broken the commandment through contempt of it, despising it as a command of God, since those who sin ignorantly break it too.

The sentence has no remedy in it, and the commentators say so plainly. Clarke states the ground — bold daring acts of transgression against the fullest evidence and in despite of the divine authority admitted of no atonement, and the presumption probably implied an utter contempt of the word and authority of God springing from an idolatrous or atheistical mind, in which case all repentance was precluded by the very denial of God's word and being. Henry puts the speech into the sinner's mouth. The language of presumptuous sin is that eternal truth is not fit to be believed, the Lord of all not fit to be obeyed, and almighty power not fit to be either feared or trusted; it imputes folly to Infinite Wisdom and iniquity to the righteous Judge of heaven and earth. Many come short of fulfilling the word and yet value it and count the law honourable; the presumptuous despise it, thinking themselves too great and too good and too wise to be ruled by it — and whatever the sin itself is, it is the contumacy that incurs the anathema. There remains no sacrifice for such sins, since the law provided none; and Henry passes on the Jewish doctors' reading of the last clause, that the iniquity cleaves to the soul after it is cut off, to be accounted for at the great day. Calvin allows that clause two senses, either confirming the justice of the punishment or warning that the impiety should be corrected betimes, before it has advanced too far.
32:
Nobody is certain when this happened. Gill reports the common Jewish view, from Aben Ezra, that though the incident is recorded here it belongs to the first year, soon after the sabbath law was given — which produces Jarchi's bitter remark that Scripture tells it to Israel's reproach, since they kept only the first sabbath and on the second this man came and profaned it. Gill himself puts it later, in the wilderness of Paran, after the spies and the discomfiture, where it stands in its proper place as an instance of the presumptuous sinner just described. Ellicott agrees, allowing only that the text says the wilderness and no more, and adding that no inference can be drawn from the verse about when the account was written down. Calvin declines to guess: since we know neither the year nor the month, nothing is better than to follow the order Moses gives. Keil reads the placement itself as the argument — the history is inserted here as a practical illustration of sinning with a high hand.

The narrative moves quickly and the commentators fill the gaps. They admonished him first, Gill says on the Targum's authority, and he would not desist; then they brought him, in Wesley's gloss, not to the whole multitude but to Moses and Aaron and the seventy rulers, and he was put in ward — in a certain prison in the camp, Gill suggests, perhaps the very one in which the blasphemer had been kept, and for much the same reason. What was uncertain was not the crime but the sentence. Wesley makes the point exactly: it was known in general that sabbath-breakers were to be put to death, and the question was in what manner he should be cut off, which God here particularly determines. Ellicott confirms it from the wording, that death had already been denounced against those who profaned the day, but the manner of inflicting it does not appear to have been declared before, and the very verb used here recurs in the parallel case of the blasphemer, whom they also put in ward that the mind of the Lord might be shewed them. Gill adds where the answer was sought: Moses consulted the Lord in the tabernacle, from above the mercy seat, where he had promised to meet him.

Calvin's reflection on the episode is unusually double-edged. The Israelites were not always affected by the same degree of madness, and here their moderation is as manifest as the fervency of their zeal — they bring the transgressor to authority rather than dealing with him themselves, they quietly wait for the decision of God, and they execute the sentence promptly once it is given. You would say that at every point they were rightly conformed to the rules of piety; and yet, since the most trifling occasion led them astray soon afterwards, their hypocrisy was betrayed by that levity. One swallow does not make a spring, and we judge a whole life wrongly from a single noble action. It may well be, Calvin adds, that the men who brought him were careless in other matters and, as hypocrites usually are, excessively rigid about an outward ceremony. From the punishment he infers that the offender had not erred through inadvertence but in gross contempt, since God would not have commanded stoning otherwise. And he draws two conclusions: that the sabbath was the mark by which God separated his people from the heathen, though its object was never mere idleness but that they should renounce their own works and live to God; and that the magistrate is appointed to maintain the first table no less than the second, since the man was not stoned by an unreflecting impulse but by the direct command of God, no political law having yet been given on the point.
37:
Ellicott corrects the picture first. These are tassels rather than fringes, set on the corners of the garment, and the garment itself was a four-cornered cloth which the poor also used as a counterpane, commonly worn with a hole in the centre for the head. Wesley describes the tassel as threads standing out further than the rest, at the four borders of the upper garment, the riband added to make it more obvious to the sight, its colour blue or purple. Gill sets out who was bound: Israelites, priests, Levites, proselytes and freed servants, but not Gentiles, who might not make them at all. Henry adds the afterlife of the custom. The Pharisees enlarged the borders — to exhibit their punctilious fulfilment of the Law, Ellicott says — and Christ wore them, which is why we read of the hem of his garment, and why the woman with the issue of blood sought it. The phylacteries, Henry insists, were a different thing altogether, of the Pharisees' own invention, whereas the fringes were a divine institution; and the Jews wear them still, saying as they put them on, blessed be he who has sanctified us unto himself and commanded us to wear fringes.

How a tassel can carry a commandment is Clarke's question, and he answers it with an argument about signs. It would be bold to assert any analogy between a fringe and a precept; but when one thing is appointed to represent another, however unlike, the first becomes the regular sign of the second. There is no analogy between the word bread and the substance it stands for, yet because the word represents the thing, everyone understands it, and the sight of it conveys not its letters but the thing signified. So with the tassels: appointed by God to bring the commandments to mind, they conveyed the intelligence intended. Calvin guards the point from the other side. There was no religion in the fringes themselves and no value in the material texture, but since men are lazy and forgetful in the cultivation of piety, God made provision for their infirmity; in telling them to look upon it and remember, he hints that they need coarse rudiments which strike the outward senses, nothing being likelier than that forgetfulness should steal upon them. Yet God has no satisfaction in empty knowledge, and demands serious affections and practical performance. Keil supplies the occasion, taking the command to have been prompted by the incident just recorded.

The clause that follows is a prohibition, and all three read it strictly. Henry sees in it a preservative from idolatry — that you seek not after your own heart and your own eyes in your religious worship — though he allows it to extend to the whole conversation, nothing being more contrary to God's honour and our own interest than to walk in the way of our heart and the sight of our eyes. Wesley gives the two errors names: enquire not for other ways of serving me than I have prescribed, neither after the devices of your own hearts, as Nadab and Abihu did when they offered strange fire, nor after the examples your eyes see, as you did when you worshipped a calf after the manner of Egypt. Calvin presses hardest. By contrasting men's hearts and eyes with his Law, God shews that he would have his people contented with the one rule he prescribes, without the admixture of their own imaginations, and denounces the vanity of whatever men invent for themselves, however pleasing. The last word of the verse makes it plain: men go a whoring whenever they are governed by their own counsels. Those who worship God by their own will account their zeal very good, and do nothing but pollute themselves with spiritual adultery; for what the world considers the holiest devotion, God with his own mouth pronounces to be fornication.
